A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same JiSi framework. Their text, equations, tables, and figures support reliable comparison. All pages were inspected, including v2 Appendices A–F; v1 ends with references and has no appendix.

before.justification: v1 reports original JiSi evaluations across nine benchmarks, baseline comparisons, cost measurements, component variants, and model-pool scaling experiments.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds evaluated baselines, component and mechanism studies, scientific-task evaluations, and qualitative cases.

M1.justification: The embedding bank, query-response-length scoring, support-set aggregator selection, and adaptive routing-aggregation switch retain the same procedure in Section 3. The new scientific-task experiments extend the bank with additional data without introducing a new algorithmic component.

E1.justification: Appendix B and Table 6 add four SGIBench task families: Wet Experiment, Dry Experiment, Deep Research, and Idea Generation. These substantially extend the original nine-benchmark coverage into scientific workflows. The multimodal subset is explicitly excluded. OpenRouterBench becoming LLMRouterBench retains the same cited commit and does not itself establish changed coverage.

E2.justification: Table 1 newly evaluates Symbolic-MoE and Self-MoA across the nine original benchmarks; v1 only discussed these methods in related work. This substantially strengthens comparison with competing routing-and-aggregation and single-model aggregation approaches. The previously evaluated external comparators remain.

E3.justification: New studies introduce a performance-estimation deviation metric, correctness-based difficulty groups, and a support-set-size sweep holding three reference responses fixed. Appendix B also specifies retaining the original embedding bank while adding scientific-task data. Original splits and judges remain. Appendix D.3 names fixed MoA/voting trios, conflicting with the retained per-benchmark selection description; this is a reporting ambiguity, not evidence that existing experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Table 5 expands the original full/router-only/no-switch comparisons into seven component configurations. Sections 4.4–4.6 add similarity-estimation, reference-filtering, and aggregator-selection analyses; Appendices E–F add three similarity cases and two aggregation-failure cases. The original model-selection distribution analysis is retained in Appendix A rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: The split seed remains 42, and Figure 5 retains its existing 95% confidence bands. No new experimental replication counts, uncertainty estimates, or significance tests are reported. Sampling within aggregation baselines is part of their inference procedure.

E6.justification: All 29 shared Table 1 rows and Table 2 cost entries are unchanged. New baseline averages are 66.89 for Symbolic-MoE and 66.52 for Self-MoA. New SGIBench results report JiSi at 27.76 versus Gemini-3-Pro at 26.00. Additional analyses include an ARS-only ablation scoring 64.87 versus 67.83 with all three components disabled. These are newly reported comparisons, not improvements to the retained main results.

T1.justification: Section 4.4 introduces the formal deviation measure 100 ||g − v||₁ / M. Section 3.3 also corrects the fine-grained model-score vector's dimension from N to M. The principal inference equations otherwise retain their substance, and no theorem or proof is added.

C1.justification: The introduction extends the demonstrated scalability claim from adding LLMs to adding both LLMs and tasks. The three core contributions and headline claim of surpassing Gemini-3-Pro while saving 53.23% of cost remain unchanged.

C2.justification: Appendix C adds the qualification that ARS alone can hurt performance without QRR and SAS. New cases explain how incorrect references can overturn a correct standalone answer, and SGIBench's multimodal exclusion makes the applicability boundary explicit. Section 4.2 softens 'theoretical performance bound' to 'strong performance bound.' The central mechanism interpretations otherwise persist.

D1.justification: Appendix D adds substantial baseline implementation information, including encoders, GraphRouter's 10,000 training epochs, RouterDC's eight A800 GPUs, batch sizes, clustering settings, and aggregation configurations. Table 7 supplies model sizes, release dates, and token prices. These are largely new disclosures, not established changes to existing runs; the original JiSi hyperparameters and access statement remain.

R1.justification: v2 adds citations to Chen et al.'s multi-LLM repeated-sampling work and Xu et al.'s SGIBench work, removes ZOOTER/Lu et al., and drops the extended positioning against SMACS's smaller-model validation. The OpenRouterBench-to-LLMRouterBench citation update represents the retained benchmark rather than a separate research lineage.

P1.justification: The introduction, related work, methodological motivation, and conclusion are substantially condensed or rewritten. Evaluation details and the original model-selection analysis move into appendices, while three diagnostic subsections enter the main experimental narrative. Terminology shifts toward 'multi-LLM,' and the author list changes.

P2.justification: v2 adds Tables 3–7, the support-set-size plot, and five boxed case-study figures. Existing ablation results are regrouped into domain summaries within the expanded Table 5. The original selection-distribution figure moves to the appendix as Figure 7, and table captions and surrounding layouts are revised. The retained leaderboard, radar, and scaling plots preserve their results.

improvement.justification: v1 provided limited component-level validation and sparse baseline implementation details. v2 substantially addresses these weaknesses through controlled mechanism studies, expanded ablations exposing an adverse component interaction, two relevant evaluated competitors, and detailed implementation reporting. Scientific-task results also broaden support for scalability. The inconsistent MoA/voting selection descriptions and loss of per-benchmark detail for the no-switch variant are drawbacks, but the gains in empirical support and reproducibility are substantial.
